view.stem: Atmospheric hydrogen molecules $\mathrm{H_2}$ and nitrogen molecules $\mathrm{N_2}$ are in local thermal equilibrium at the same temperature. Use the classical molecular thermal-motion model. Which statements about their root-mean-square speeds and mean translational kinetic energies hold?

options.text: The two species have equal mean translational kinetic energies.
Every hydrogen molecule is faster than every nitrogen molecule.
Hydrogen molecules have the greater root-mean-square speed.
Nitrogen molecules have the greater root-mean-square speed.

intent.task: Compare characteristic molecular speeds while distinguishing a speed statistic, average translational energy, and a claim about every individual molecule.
intent.source_solution: Reuse frozen source-solutions-complete.json task1. At common T, m*overline(v^2)=3k_B*T, so v_rms=sqrt(3k_B*T/m). H2 is lighter than N2 and has greater RMS speed, with approximate ratio sqrt(28/2)=sqrt(14). Both species have mean translational energy (3/2)k_B*T. The distributions overlap, so no every-molecule ordering follows. Without common T the ordering depends on T_H2/T_N2 versus m_H2/m_N2. Common temperature is a visible added condition, not a quoted source fact. RMS is separately named here; task4's historical mean squared speed is not redefined.
intent.unit_reason: One multiple-response item tests the coherent same-temperature mass-and-motion comparison and its limits; the two species are not converted into isolated clicks.
limitations: Recognition does not demonstrate writing an independent molecular-motion derivation.
The original faster comparison did not specify a statistic or common temperature; the stem explicitly selects RMS speed and classical common-temperature equilibrium.
Average-energy and individual-quantifier judgments clarify this same comparison; they are additional judgments, not extra source data.

rationales.derivation: Mean translational kinetic energy is (1/2)m*overline(v^2)=(3/2)k_B*T, independent of molecular mass at the common T.
Start with the true inequality of RMS speeds and replace it with an inequality for all individual pairs. Classical speed distributions overlap: a slow H2 molecule and a faster N2 molecule can occur.
rationales.misconception: Promote an inequality between statistical measures to a universal ordering of individuals.

rationales.derivation: v_rms=sqrt(3k_B*T/m); at equal T, m_H2<m_N2 implies v_rms,H2>v_rms,N2. Approximate molar masses 2 and 28 g/mol give ratio sqrt(14).
Mis-solve m*v_rms^2=3k_B*T as v_rms^2=(3k_B*T)*m instead of dividing by m. The resulting false sqrt(m) dependence places the heavier N2 ahead.
rationales.misconception: Multiply by molecular mass instead of dividing when solving for the squared speed.

intent.task: Use the actual p-V and V-T graphs and the original isothermal definition to determine every one of the five requested energy changes.
intent.source_solution: The first actual-image derivation was frozen in graph-source-derivation.json before options or book answers. Original n30 neglects intermolecular interaction; n36 relates fixed-gas internal energy to absolute temperature, not independently to volume. Figure24 moves right at fixed p, so pV=nuRT gives T1'>T1. Original n17 explicitly identifies 1'->2 as isothermal, giving T2=T1'. The opened Figure30 has T2=T3>T1 with arrows 1->2, 2->3, 3->1. The complete five-change sequence is increase, unchanged, increase, unchanged, decrease. No monatomic coefficient is imposed and no numerical ratio is taken from pixels.
intent.unit_reason: One complete table retains all five judgments and the common principle across two coordinate systems without per-segment clicks or an earlier graph item revealing a later answer.
limitations: Recognizing a complete table does not demonstrate writing the five derivations.
The two panels are separate physical paths; equal state numbers do not bind one sample across panels.
Unscaled graphs determine signs, not numerical energy changes or ratios.
Isothermality comes from the original n17 definition, not a curve's appearance. Fixed amount/composition and the classical model are visible conditions.

figure_observations.observation: Opened the full original PNG first, then its complete 640x576 preview bound to the installed SVG bytes. Vertical p, horizontal V; p2>p1 and V1<V2<V'. The arrow 1->1' is rightward and 1'->2 follows the upper curve left/up. All state guides and rightmost/bottommost labels are visible. No scale. Isotherm identity comes from original prose.

Opened the full original PNG first, then its complete 640x704 preview bound to the installed SVG. Vertical V, horizontal T; dashed origin extension through1, ray1->2 right/up, vertical2->3 downward, horizontal3->1 leftward. T2=T3>T1 and V2>V3=V1. Full bottom/right axis labels visible; no numerical scale.

rationales.derivation: Falsely set U proportional to V. Reading directed V changes gives Figure24 increase/decrease and Figure30 increase/decrease/unchanged, exactly tableA. Isothermal compression need not reduce U; constant-volume cooling does reduce U.
rationales.misconception: Replace temperature dependence of a fixed gas's internal energy with volume dependence.

rationales.derivation: Fixed-gas U increases with T. Figure24 first raises T by increasing V at constant p, then keeps T constant by the original isothermal definition. Figure30's T coordinate increases, stays fixed, then decreases. Hence increase, unchanged, increase, unchanged, decrease.

Read T for noncompression segments, but falsely assume all compression is adiabatic with Delta U=W_on>0. Overwrite both isothermal compression segments, Figure24 1'->2 and Figure30 2->3, to obtain increase/increase/increase/increase/decrease. Heat can leave during isothermal compression.
rationales.misconception: Treat isothermal compression as adiabatic and omit the heat needed to keep temperature fixed.

rationales.derivation: Falsely set U proportional to p alone. Figure24 has constant/increasing p. Figure30's origin ray has constant V/T and hence constant p, its downward vertical raises p at fixed T, and its leftward horizontal lowers p at fixed V. This gives tableD.
rationales.misconception: Use pressure alone as an energy indicator, dropping volume from the state relation.

view.stem: At $20^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and standard atmospheric pressure $p=101325\ \mathrm{Pa}$, a room holds $50\ \mathrm{m^3}$ of air and a glass holds $200\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of liquid water. Treat air as ideal gas. Use water density $1000\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}$, water molar mass $0.018\ \mathrm{kg/mol}$, $R=8.314\ \mathrm{J/(mol\,K)}$, and $T=t+273.15\ \mathrm{K}$. Count only air molecules and the molecules of water in the glass. With $r=N_{\rm air}/N_{\rm water}$, which comparison is correct?

options.text: $r\approx2.5\times10^5$; the room air contains more molecules.
$r\approx187$; the room air contains more molecules.

intent.task: Compare total molecule counts in a gas and a liquid, rather than number density or volume alone.
intent.source_solution: Reuse frozen task3. nu_air=pV/(RT) approximately2079mol. Water volume is200*10^-6=2*10^-4m3, mass0.2kg, and amount0.2/0.018 approximately11.11mol. N_A cancels in r=[pV/(RT)]/[rho*V_water/M], approximately187. The counts are about1.25*10^27 air molecules and6.69*10^24 water molecules. Do not apply an ideal-gas equation to liquid water. Added material constants and the counting scope are visible assumptions, not source-given exact data.
intent.unit_reason: The ratio and total-count comparison form one complete result requiring both phase models, not isolated unit-conversion and molar-count clicks.
limitations: Recognition does not demonstrate writing independent gas/liquid counting derivations.
The result uses declared ideal-air and approximate liquid-water properties, not exact experimental counts derivable solely from the source prose.

rationales.derivation: Compute N_water/N_air=1/187.08 approximately0.00535 but keep the defined label r=N_air/N_water, then incorrectly interpret r<1 as more water molecules.
rationales.misconception: Invert numerator and denominator without changing the stated ratio definition.

rationales.derivation: Assume equal molecular number densities for air and water. The false total-count ratio becomes the volume ratio50/(200*10^-6)=250000, ignoring both physical density models.
rationales.misconception: Treat different phases as having equal molecule number density and compare volumes alone.

rationales.derivation: Convert200cm3 incorrectly to200*10^-3=0.2m3. Water mass becomes200kg,1000times too large; r becomes187.08/1000 approximately0.187, producing0.19 and the wrong ordering.
rationales.misconception: Use10^-3 instead of10^-6 for the cm3-to-m3 conversion.

view.stem: Water molecules in blood warm from $37^\circ\mathrm{C}$ to $40^\circ\mathrm{C}$. The source-defined mean-square speed is $\overline{v^2}$, in $\mathrm{m^2/s^2}$, not its square root. Use the classical translational thermal-equilibrium model for the same molecular species and $T=t+273.15\ \mathrm{K}$. By what percentage does the mean-square speed increase relative to its initial value?

intent.task: Apply the original n32 mean squared speed definition and the initial absolute-temperature denominator to calculate percentage increase.
intent.source_solution: Reuse frozen task4 and source-definition-context.json. Original p=(1/3)m*n_density*overline(v^2) defines the historical quantity as overline(v^2), not its square root. Classical translational equilibrium gives overline(v^2)=3k_B*T/m for a fixed species. T_initial=310.15K, T_final=313.15K, so percentage increase=(3/310.15)*100%=0.9672739%, approximately0.97%. This is a thermal translational model for liquid molecules, not an ideal-gas pressure equation applied to blood.
intent.unit_reason: One complete percentage calculation preserves the quantity definition, temperature conversion and initial-value denominator without splitting its arithmetic steps.
limitations: Recognition does not demonstrate establishing the equilibrium relation independently.
The classical translational model is explicit; blood is not modeled as ideal gas.
Mean squared speed and RMS are distinguished; no source erratum is claimed.

rationales.derivation: Replace the requested quantity by RMS speed and compute[sqrt(313.15/310.15)-1]*100% approximately0.4825%, rounding to0.48%. That answers the increase of the square root instead.
rationales.misconception: Substitute the square root for the original mean squared speed.

rationales.derivation: Convert temperatures correctly but divide the increase by the final value:3/313.15*100%=0.9580073%, rounding to0.96%, instead of dividing by310.15.
rationales.misconception: Use the final rather than the initial value as the percentage-increase denominator.

rationales.derivation: For the same molecular mass, overline(v^2) is proportional to T. (313.15-310.15)/310.15*100%=0.9672739%, rounding to0.97%.
Use Celsius values directly: (40-37)/37*100%=8.1081%, rounding to8.11%. The denominator37 is not an absolute temperature.
rationales.misconception: Use a Celsius temperature ratio in a proportionality requiring absolute temperature.

view.stem: A vacuum pump reduces pressure to $p=1.3\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{Pa}$, approximately $10^{-12}$ mm of mercury. At $27^\circ\mathrm{C}$, how many molecules are present on average in $1\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of residual gas? Use ideal-gas thermal equilibrium, $k_B=1.380649\times10^{-23}\ \mathrm{J/K}$, and $T=t+273.15\ \mathrm{K}$. Calculate with the stated SI pressure.

intent.task: Find the expected total molecular count at very low pressure in a specified small volume using SI pressure, absolute temperature and cubic-volume conversion.
intent.source_solution: Reuse frozen task5. Combine p=(1/3)m*n_density*overline(v^2) with m*overline(v^2)=3k_B*T to obtain p=n_density*k_B*T. N=pV/(k_B*T)=(1.3*10^-10*10^-6)/(1.380649*10^-23*300.15)=31370.52, approximately3.1*10^4. Molecular mass cancels. This is a macroscopic-average or expected count, not an exact instantaneous integer census. The mercury pressure is source-rounded, not an additional exact constraint.
intent.unit_reason: One complete expected count retains the physical scale and unit conversion, distinct from the phase-model comparison in the air/water item.
limitations: Recognition does not demonstrate independent derivation or exponent arithmetic.
The declared ideal-gas result is an average count, not an exact instantaneous integer or a higher-precision experimental result.

rationales.derivation: Convert volume correctly but use T=27:1.3*10^-16/(1.380649*10^-23*27)=3.487*10^5, rounding to3.5*10^5.
rationales.misconception: Use Celsius in place of absolute temperature in the gas relation.

rationales.derivation: Apply the length factor only once, writing1cm3=10^-2m3 instead of(10^-2)^3m3. The count becomes10^4 times too large,3.137*10^8, rounding to3.1*10^8.
rationales.misconception: Fail to cube the linear centimeter-to-meter conversion factor for a volume.

rationales.derivation: Omit cubic-centimeter conversion and substitute V=1 into the SI equation:1.3*10^-10/(1.380649*10^-23*300.15)=3.137*10^10, rounding to3.1*10^10.
rationales.misconception: Treat one cubic centimeter as one cubic meter.

view.stem: One adiabatic compressor stroke compresses $4\ \mathrm{mol}$ of monatomic ideal gas. Here $500\ \mathrm{J}$ explicitly means net compression work received by the gas, $W_{\rm on}=+500\ \mathrm{J}$, not positive work done by the gas or the compressor's gross energy expenditure. The gas is a closed system with no other energy transfers and negligible changes in macroscopic kinetic or potential energy. Use $R=8.314\ \mathrm{J/(mol\,K)}$. What is the temperature change $\Delta T$?

intent.task: Apply the adiabatic closed-gas energy balance after explicitly fixing work actor, sign and net energy transfer.
intent.source_solution: Reuse frozen task6. The original work of500J does not specify actor, sign or net transfer fraction, so the source solution remains conditional. If500J is net work on the gas, Delta U=Q+W_on=+500J; monatomic gas has Delta U=(3/2)*nu*R*Delta T, giving Delta T=500/(6R) approximately+10.0K for4mol. If it is signed positive W_by, Delta U=-500J and Delta T approximately-10.0K, inconsistent with ordinary passive compression. Gross compressor energy alone gives no numerical gas temperature change without losses/partition. The visible stem selects net input; it does not universally resolve the source ambiguity.
intent.unit_reason: Temperature change is one complete energy-balance result. Necessary sign and transfer conditions are disclosed, not turned into repeated heat/work/coefficient subquestions.
limitations: Recognition does not demonstrate independently writing the first law.
The original work actor and sign remain ambiguous; this item assesses only the visible net-work-input model.
Initial temperature is absent, so final absolute temperature is not determined. No constant-volume or reversible path is required.

rationales.derivation: Use monatomic C_p=(5/2)R in place of the internal-energy coefficient C_v=(3/2)R:500=(5/2)*4*8.314*Delta T. This gives500/83.14=6.014K, approximately+6.0K.
rationales.misconception: Use the enthalpy temperature coefficient for the closed gas's internal-energy change.

rationales.derivation: Insert the stated+500J work-on value as W_by=+500J into Delta U=Q-W_by, giving Delta U=-500J and Delta T=-10.023K. Correct conversion is W_by=-500J. This is incorrect under the visible stem; the original's other signed reading remains honestly recorded internally.
rationales.misconception: Use positive work on the gas as positive work by the gas without changing actor and sign.

rationales.derivation: Q=0 and W_on=+500J give Delta U=500J. Delta U=(3/2)*4*8.314*Delta T=49.884*Delta T, so Delta T=500/49.884=10.023K, approximately+10.0K.
Infer Delta U=0 from adiabatic Q=0, dropping500J of work, then use Delta U=6R*Delta T to obtain Delta T=0.
rationales.misconception: Equate absence of heat transfer with absence of internal-energy change and omit work.
